Germs in the recalled food could spread to drawers or shelves in your refrigerator. What you need Sealable bags Hot, soapy water Clean towels Bleach (optional) How to clean your refrigerator Steps to take Throw out recalled food and any other foods stored with it or touching it Put the recalled food in a sealed bag in the garbage. Empty your refrigerator Empty the rest of the items in your refrigerator and put them on a counter or table while you clean. Take out shelving, drawers, and any other removable parts. pages.text: How to Experience St Moritz’s Snow Polo World Cup Weekend | National Geographic By Emma Al-Mousawi Published November 14, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). For one weekend in late January, frozen Lake St Moritz, encircled by Switzerland’s snow-heaped Engadin Alps, becomes the glittering stage for one of polo’s most prestigious events: the Snow Polo World Cup St Moritz. Sunglass-clad spectators in cashmere, elegant coats and designer puffer jackets gather as champagne flutes clink and oysters are shucked. On the ice, six teams of white-slacked players thunder across the 200-metre pitch, competing for the coveted trophy against the dazzling backdrop of one of Europe’s oldest and most exclusive ski resorts. Polo traces its origins back more than two millennia to the grasslands of Persia, but its snowy incarnation is decidedly younger. It was conceived here just over 40 years ago by Reto Gaudenzi, a local player and founder of Switzerland’s first polo team. Undeterred by the fact that polo had never been played on snow, he experimented with hoof grips and a larger, slower orange ball. A successful trial followed in 1984; a year later, the world’s first snow polo tournament was staged on the lake before more than 1,000 spectators. Today, the three-day event draws crowds of 26,000 — and dozens of private jets. pages.text: How to Explore the Indian Ocean Through Its Spices | National Geographic By Daniel Stables Published September 19, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Nowadays, most of us take spices for granted — a pinch of cinnamon in porridge, black pepper over pasta or cumin stirred into a curry. Yet for centuries these everyday ingredients shaped the course of history. The trade in black pepper facilitated cultural and economic intermixing between ancient Rome and India, while camels pulled frankincense caravans across the deserts that separated Africa and Asia, taking with them ideas, recipes, music and language. Today, these influences can still be felt in many countries, offering a fascinating, and often delicious, theme through which to explore a place. Browse the Spice Souks of Muscat, Oman Located on the Arabian Sea between Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the UAE, the seafaring nation of Oman has long been a link between East Africa, India and Southeast Asia. That story is told in the spice section of Muttrah Souk, the Omani capital’s historic covered market, where technicolour cones of powdered ginger, turmeric and cumin sit alongside piles of frankincense rocks, bundled strands of saffron, and less familiar items like loomi — black, sun-dried limes. The air hangs particularly heavy with the scent of frankincense, which Omanis use to perfume their homes, cars and traditional robes. pages.text: How to Explore the Pantanal | National Geographic A school of fish and a hungry caiman in the waters of the Pantanal region Photograph by Luciano Candisani, National Geographic TRAVEL How to Explore the Pantanal Explore the Pantanal from all corners with this guide to the beauty of this national park and UNESCO World Heritage site. By Avery Stonich Published August 4, 2016 • 4 min read The Pantanal is the world’s largest wetland , pooling over 81,000 square miles (210,000 square kilometers)—an area nearly the size of Kansas—in the center of South America, mostly in central-western Brazil and straddling the borders of Paraguay and Bolivia. Often overshadowed by the Amazon to the north, the Pantanal quietly harbors the highest concentration of wildlife in South America . The traditional Okinawan sabani boats were historically used for fishing and travelling between islands. Photograph by James Whitlow Delano By Georgia Stephens Published January 7, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). It’s show time. Up heaves the sail, a concertina of heavy canvas pulled taut against the creaking wooden mast. It gulps the breeze that’s whisking cotton puffs of cloud out to sea. Black butterflies, big as sparrows, rise from the steep jungle at our backs as the droning of cicadas meets the surf raking the beach. The air is flower-scented, hot and heavy as water. Up comes the anchor, out come the paddles; the nose of the traditional sabani boat plunges into the waves. Any sailor leaving Ishigaki island needs to be absolutely certain of their course. Head north west, and the next landfall lies hundreds of miles away in China; east, and it’ll be the considerably farther-flung shores of Mexico. Here, in southern Okinawa Prefecture, Japan fizzles out in a spray of its remotest isles. Closer to Taiwan and the Philippines than the mainland and fed by warmer currents, the subtropical Yaeyama Islands, of which Ishigaki is a part, are unique within Japan. On 11 November, Vienna’s palaces and music halls kick into high gear. Dance floors swarm with couples waltzing in choreographed swirls — and freestyling to live electropop. The two scenes are complementary halves of the Austrian capital’s modern ball scene: an old custom attracting new attention, buoyed by social media and miles of bias-cut silk. The festivities trace their roots to the 1700s, when Emperor Joseph II opened the Hofburg Palace dances — until then, reserved for nobility — to ordinary citizens. The decision paved the way for a wider ball culture to develop in the following centuries. Help for Survey Participants How We Conduct Our Surveys In addition to conducting the decennial census count, the Census Bureau conducts various surveys that study households, businesses, schools, hospitals, and more. The Census Bureau will notify you in advance if you are in a survey, provide different ways to respond, and may follow up with you. We notify you if you are in a survey. The U.S. Census Bureau typically sends an official letter describing the survey for which your household or business has been selected and why your participation is important. This letter describes what the survey is, what type of questions will be asked, and what you can expect as a survey participant. For household surveys, most mailings from the Census Bureau are addressed to “the resident of.” Household surveys from the Census Bureau are only mailed to residential addresses, not to P.O. Boxes. P.O. Boxes are not associated with specific addresses, so the Census Bureau cannot use them as a mailing destination. If you are visited by a field representative working on a survey and have not yet received a survey letter or notice from the Census Bureau, you can request one from the representative at your door. You may also contact the Census Bureau Regional Office for your state for more information. Some surveys send invitations via text message or email. pages.text: Hull man and wife who fled Ukraine return to a warzone Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live 'Friends think we're idiots for returning to Ukraine' 21 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Kevin Shoesmith East Yorkshire and Lincolnshire John Holmes Liliya Holmes and her British husband John pictured in Odesa, Ukraine When Russian forces launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, John Holmes – a British national – and his Ukrainian wife Liliya fled the port city of Odesa, fearing for their lives. But after four years in the UK, the draw of home has proven too strong and they have returned to Ukraine's third largest city, undeterred by the sustained threat of air raids. "Friends of ours thought we were idiots for going back to Ukraine," reflects John, 74. "But returning is something we felt we needed to do. "Yes, it's dangerous. Yes, there are drones flying overhead. Yes, you can hear the explosions. But you just have to get on with life as best you can. "Home is Ukraine." During their time away, the pair sought sanctuary in Hull , East Yorkshire, where John was born and raised and has a property. He met Liliya, 64, in Ukraine and had been living there for 30 years until the invasion. "We had built a good life here," he says. Human factors analysis can be used to advance our understanding of the true nature of errors in complex work settings. Research in this area has identified factors that contribute to inefficiencies and quantified the effects of human and organizational factors on performance of critical tasks. The forensic science community can benefit from the application of the substantial body of human factors work to reduce the likelihood and consequences of human error in the scientific interpretation of evidence. To assist the forensic community in this effort, the National Institute of Justice (NIJ) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Special Programs Office partnered to develop a series of expert panels to examine human factors in forensic analyses and develop practices to reduce the likelihood of error based on scientific research. It’s a colloquial term in the outdoor community. You see it everywhere, from campground signage to park brochures, and wilderness permits to ranger programs. It’s intermingled with phrases like “pack it in, pack it out” and “take only photos.” Leave No Trace has become so common in the outdoor community, that many forget that not everyone knows what it means. If you’ve found yourself staring blankly at a ranger saying, “Remember to Leave No Trace” as they send you on your way—this article is for you. Did You Know? Leave No Trace is a set of principles that empower people visiting the outdoors to leave nature as unchanged by our presence as possible. It’s a way of protecting the natural world to keep our outdoor spaces enjoyable for generations to come. "There's a pivotal scene in a prison yard, and we're singing Silent Night with the Ghost of Christmas Present and Johnny Depp there," recalls Bedfordshire's Colin Fraser. Depp plays the title character Ebenezer Scrooge in the Charles Dickens tale, starring alongside Rupert Grint, Sir Ian McKellen and Daisy Ridley. Fraser, 55, who has appeared in West End shows such as The Lion King, landed his current role when London Voices, his choir, was asked to audition for the film. He says that despite the spooky setting, the renditions of Silent Night and other carols are "completely straight" and "very traditional". "We sang them traditionally in four-part harmony as we would every year," he says. These inventories provide baseline information from which additional monitoring activities are conducted. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Idaho Falls District Office The Idaho Falls District, located in southeast Idaho, manages approximately 3.7 million acres of public land. The topography and terrain differ substantially throughout the area, ranging from sagebrush and desert to high-elevation forests. The District itself incorporates 16 counties, with Montana to the north and Utah to the south. The western edge borders the Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, with the eastern edge extending to the beautiful Teton mountain range. With such a diverse geographic area, the Idaho Falls District has many challenges to face as it balances its mission of multiple use and sustainable yield to achieve a sustainable ecosystem. Some of the major activities occurring within the district include: grazing, recreation, mining, wildlife and fisheries, fire management, riparian and wetland management, realty and land use. The Idaho Falls District is divided into four geographic areas/field offices: Challis (799,000 acres), Salmon (493,000 acres), Upper Snake (1,854,000 acres) and Pocatello (557,000 acres).
